issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, sexual-violence comments as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless the index event also involved sexual assault or closely related content; nothing else in the profile supports that connection.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is difficult to fit with terrorism as the trauma type unless there was a clear interpersonal betrayal component; the rest of the selected items describe loss of control, helplessness, avoidance, dissociation, and substance use rather than interpersonal betrayal.

vignette:
Ravi leaned forward in the chair, his hands clasped tightly in his lap, and began to speak. He was a clinical psychologist, thirty-seven years old, married, with a practice of his own. He knew the diagnostic criteria by heart, had administered the CAPS-5 to dozens of patients, and yet here he was, describing a night that had rewritten the rules of his life.

It had happened three years ago, during a late summer evening in a city he had chosen for its quiet safety. He had been walking home from a corner store, a bag of groceries in one hand, his phone in the other, when a single gunshot cracked the air. It was not near him—maybe a block away, maybe two—but the sound had been sharp and absolute, a punctuation mark that ended one version of the world and started another. He had frozen, then run, not toward the sound but away, into an alley, pressing himself against a brick wall, heart hammering, waiting for the next shot. The police arrived, and later he learned it had been a domestic dispute, a man shooting at his wife, no one killed. But for Ravi, that single second had carved a groove into his mind that would not let go.

In the weeks that followed, he began to notice changes. He had always been someone who believed in his own agency—a therapist who helped others reclaim control over their lives. Now, a quiet dread had settled in. He found himself thinking, with a certainty that felt like fact, that he could not stop bad things from happening. The world, he now understood, was a dangerous place. The belief was not intellectual; it was visceral, a cold weight in his chest when he stepped outside. He began to avoid anything that could be stressful. He stopped taking new clients with complex trauma histories, citing a full caseload. He stopped driving on highways, then on busy streets, then stopped driving altogether after dark. He told his wife he was tired, that he needed more rest. At night, he would lie awake, listening to the house settle, to the creak of the floorboards, to the wind against the window. Waking up in the dark became its own terror—a moment of disorientation, the world not yet solid, and the thought that something terrible could be waiting.

He started drinking. A glass of wine became two, then three, then a full bottle some nights, just to get to sleep. On worse nights, he took one of the old prescription pills he had kept from a past surgery. He knew it was a problem. He was a psychologist; he had written treatment plans for substance use. But the drinking and the medication were not about pleasure—they were about escape. And when that escape was not enough, he would drift. He would be sitting in his office, a patient speaking, and he would let his mind slide away into a world of his own, a quiet place where there were no gunshots, no darkness, no sense of being watched. The fantasies were not elaborate; they were just safe. He would imagine a beach at dusk, the sound of waves, no one around. But coming back to the room, to the patient’s waiting face, was jarring. He would feel a surge of shame, a sense that the person he had become was unrecognisable. He had been a competent clinician, a steady husband, a man who helped others. Now he was someone who drank alone, who avoided his own life, who could not even sit through a session without fleeing into his own mind.

His wife noticed. She asked him, gently, what was wrong. He told her he was just tired, overworked. She did not push, but the distance between them grew. He stopped going out to dinner with her, stopped joining her for evening walks. He would sit in the living room, lights on, television playing, waiting for the night to end. The avoidance had become a cage, and he had built it himself.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of professional failure. A new patient, a young woman who had witnessed a shooting, sat in his office and described the sound of the gunshot. Ravi felt his chest tighten, his vision narrow. He could not breathe. He excused himself, went to the bathroom, and stood over the sink, shaking. He realized he could not treat her. He could not treat anyone. He referred her to a colleague and closed his practice the next day.

Now, sitting in a therapist’s office for the first time as a patient, Ravi is afraid. He is afraid of what he will find, afraid that the person he has become is permanent, afraid that the world is as dangerous as he now believes. But he is also tired—tired of the drinking, the drifting, the hiding. He wants to stop. He wants to know if it is possible to come back.
